title: The announcer reads the other name
allegory: A name mover is a stadium announcer at the final microphone: told not to read the name that came up twice, he looks over at the other name card and reads it out, and the harder he looks at a card, the louder that name comes out.

chapters.name: Who says Mary?
chapters.note: someone has to actually say the name

props.label: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to

cap.1: 'When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to...' GPT-2 small says Mary. Some part of the model has to find Mary and say her name. Which part?
cap.2: IOI prompts end at 'to'; the answer is the indirect object. Direct logit attribution over all 144 heads points at a few late heads writing the answer: 9.6, 9.9 and 10.0.
cap.3: DLA on logit[IO] − logit[S] at END singles out 9.6, 9.9 and 10.0 as positive direct contributors, while 10.7 and 11.10 stand out negatively (Wang et al., 2022).

cap.1: Picture a stadium announcer at the last microphone. He glances at one name card and reads it out. Where he looks picks the name; the microphone just repeats it.
cap.2: A name mover attends from the last token back to a name, then its OV circuit copies that name into the logits. Attention picks the name; OV does the copying.
cap.3: Name movers attend END to IO (QK side), and their OV circuits map the attended name token onto its own unembedding direction: attention selects, OV copies.

cap.1: The harder the announcer looks at a card, the louder that name comes out. Plot where he looks against what he says, and the two rise together.
cap.2: The writing-direction check: per prompt, plot attention on a name against the head's output dotted with that name's unembedding. For name movers they rise together (idealised here).
cap.3: Projection of the head output onto W_U[name] grows with attention probability on that name; the real result is a scatter, drawn here as a line. It is the signature of OV copying.

parts.note: from the name it looks at

cap.1: Why does looking at Mary make it say Mary? Its inner microphone maps each name it looks at onto that same name in the output: a copying machine.
cap.2: Multiply embedding, the head's OV matrix and unembedding and you get a name-to-name table. For a copier, each row's biggest entry is on the diagonal: name in, same name out.
cap.3: The full OV circuit W_U W_OV W_E is vocab-by-vocab; a copying head has diagonal-dominant rows. Heads sharing an attention pattern should be scored together: their sum is the circuit.

chapters.name: The understudies
chapters.verdict: A small ablation effect does not mean a small role.

cap.1: Knock out the announcer and an understudy grabs the microphone. The answer barely changes, so the announcer looks unimportant. He was not.
cap.2: Ablate a name mover and backup name movers take over, so the logit difference drops less than the head's real contribution. Single-head ablation understates importance.
cap.3: Backup name movers compensate when primaries are ablated, so ablation effects are not contributions; and negative name movers 10.7 and 11.10 write against the answer outright.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The last step of the IOI relay

cap.1: Name movers are where the model's reasoning turns into a word. Find the heads that say the answer, then trace backwards to see why.
cap.2: IOI in week 8 is where you practise DLA, patching and ablation on real heads. Name movers are the first heads you find, and their backups teach you to distrust single ablations.
cap.3: Output-side heads anchor circuit analysis and steering alike: locate who writes the answer, then trace upstream through Q, K and V composition to understand or steer the behaviour.

params.label: ablate the primary name mover (0 off, 1 on)

readouts.label: what the ablation suggests
readouts.f: 3 - 3*backup < 1.5 ? 'the primary looks minor (wrongly)' : 'the primary looks important'

caption.1: Flip the ablation on, then turn up the backups. The total barely drops even though the primary was doing all the work.
caption.2: Toy units: the primary writes 3.0 toward Mary. Ablate it and backups refill part of that. The measured drop is 3 × (1 − backup), not the primary's real 3.0.
caption.3: Ablation measures total effect under compensation, not direct contribution. Pair it with DLA or path patching, and check for backups before calling a head unimportant.

where_else: Induction heads: the same look-then-copy move, keyed on what came next last time
Copy mechanisms in summarisation models: attend to a source word, then copy it out
Any circuit hunt: find the heads that write the answer first, then trace back

hamming.what: A late attention head that attends from the final token to the name that was not repeated and copies it into the output logits.
hamming.when: When you study the IOI circuit in week 8, and whenever you look for the heads that directly write a model's answer.
hamming.why: It is where the circuit's reasoning becomes output, so it is the natural place to start tracing, and the classic lesson in why ablation can hide a role.

object.title: The pointing announcer
object.subtitle: Each dot is the head's output on one sentence; it lands along the arrow of whichever name the head looked at.

clusters.label: outputs when it looked at Mary
outputs when it looked at John

cap.1: Each dot is what the head wrote on one sentence. When it looked at Mary, the dot lands out along Mary's arrow.
cap.2: Head outputs at END, one per prompt. Attending to Mary puts the output along W_U[Mary].
cap.3: Output vectors cluster along the unembedding direction of the attended name: OV copying seen in the residual space.

cap.1: When it looked at John instead, the dot lands along John's arrow. The output points wherever the attention went.
cap.2: Attend to S and the output points along W_U[S]; the same OV map, applied to a different name.
cap.3: The OV circuit is shared across names: the output direction is a function of which token was attended.

cap.1: Split attention gives an output in between. The more it looks at a name, the further along that name's arrow it lands.
cap.2: Mixed attention gives a weighted mix of the two directions: attention probability sets how far along each arrow.
cap.3: Head output is the attention-weighted sum of OV-mapped values, hence the writing-direction correlation.

cap.1: A name's score is how far the output reaches along that name's arrow. That is why looking at Mary raises Mary's score.
cap.2: A logit is a dot product with W_U[name], so reaching along Mary's arrow raises logit[Mary] and the logit difference.
cap.3: Logit contribution = output · W_U[name]; for IOI we read the projection onto W_U[IO] − W_U[S].

predict.q: What decides which name a name mover writes?
predict.why: OV copies whatever it attends to; attention picks which name that is.

predict.q: You ablate name mover 9.9 and the logit difference barely drops. Conclusion?

options.t: Not proven unimportant: backups may be compensating

predict.why: Backup name movers take over when primaries are ablated, so single-head ablation understates importance.

predict.q: The more a name mover attends to Mary, the more its output...
predict.why: That is the writing-direction result: attention on a name tracks the output's projection onto that name's unembedding.
